c.tagline: Where volcano meets sea in the heart of the Indian Ocean.

taxi.fareNote: Shared taxis (taxis collectifs) run set in-town routes for a fixed per-seat fare; private/whole-car hires are negotiated up front since meters are not used.

emergency.note: Emergency response can be slow and under-resourced; serious medical cases are often referred to private clinics (e.g., Clinique Al-Amal) or evacuated to Réunion/Madagascar. Fire brigade can be reached at +269 772 03 73.

hood_landmark.Coulée: Stade Omnisports Said Mohamed Cheikh, Moroni

hood_desc: The historic walled old town of narrow coral-stone lanes around the Friday Mosque and the port; suits culture-focused travelers who want to be within walking distance of the market, mosques and ferries.
Moroni's loudest, most commercial quarter, built around the city's largest open-air market; a good low-cost base for backpackers who don't mind noise and want to be near shared-taxi stands.
The port and seafront corniche district with fishing boats and a coastal promenade, a short walk from the old town; suits travelers wanting central, mid-range hotels near the harbor.
A quieter beach quarter a few kilometers north of downtown with black volcanic-sand beaches and Moroni's main resort-style hotels; ideal for travelers prioritizing pools, sea views and comfort.
A residential district built on an old lava flow near the national stadium, home to guesthouses and long-stay apartments; suits longer-term visitors wanting a calmer, local feel away from downtown.

The southern residential quarter around Hamramba and Boulevard Karthala, about 2 km from the old town, where most of Moroni's larger modern hotels and long-stay guesthouses are; suits business visitors and anyone wanting parking and a quiet room away from the medina's lanes.

water.note: Tap water is unsafe for tourists; drink bottled or filtered water.

transit.pay: Cash only (Comorian francs); shared-taxi and minibus fares are paid in cash directly to the driver or a fare collector, with per-seat prices fixed by route. There is no card or app-based payment system.
transit.hours: No fixed timetables; shared taxis and minibuses run through daylight hours and largely stop before sunset, with little to no service after dark.
transit.note: There is no formal urban transit network; getting around relies on shared taxis, private taxi hire, or walking in the compact city center.

bus: Minibuses to towns and villages (no fixed schedule)
ferry: Maria Galanta ferry to Anjouan and Mayotte (twice weekly)
Cargo/passenger boats to other islands and mainland Africa

airport.name: Prince Said Ibrahim International Airport (HAH)
rentals: No major international chains; a few small local car-hire agencies operate near the airport and in town

transit.m: Shared taxi/minibus into Moroni (~30 min, shared)

tip.r: Tipping is not obligatory or deeply rooted locally, but rounding up bills or leaving a small tip at upscale hotels and restaurants catering to foreigners is appreciated.

landmarks: Ancienne Mosquée du Vendredi (Old Friday Mosque)
This centuries-old whitewashed mosque with its slender minaret overlooking the harbor is Moroni's most photographed landmark and a striking symbol of Comorian Islamic heritage.
Volcan Karthala
One of the world's largest active volcanoes looms over Grande Comore, and adventurous hikers can trek to its immense, otherworldly caldera for sweeping island views.
La Corniche (Moroni Waterfront)
This palm-lined seaside promenade buzzes at sunset with fishermen, vendors, and families, offering postcard views of traditional wooden boats bobbing against the Indian Ocean.
Grand Marché de Moroni (Voidjou Market)
A vibrant, chaotic market where vanilla, cloves, ylang-ylang, and colorful textiles pile high, giving visitors a sensory dive into everyday Comorian life.
Place de France
This central square, framed by old colonial buildings, is a favorite spot to watch daily life unfold and catch a cool ocean breeze in the heart of the capital.
Palais du Peuple (Beit Salam)
The Comorian presidential palace's grand white facade overlooking the sea makes it one of the most recognizable government buildings in the country.
Itsandra Beach and Palace Ruins
Just north of the capital, this palm-fringed beach hides the crumbling ruins of a former sultan's palace, blending relaxed swimming with a touch of royal history.
Chomoni Beach
Powdery white sand and calm turquoise water make this beach, framed by the volcanic slopes behind it, one of Grande Comore's most beautiful escapes.
Lac Salé (Salt Lake)
A striking crater lake near Bangoi-Kouni fills with seawater seeping through volcanic rock, creating an eerily still, turquoise pool ringed by dark cliffs.
National Museum of the Comoros
A compact but worthwhile museum showcasing traditional Comorian artifacts, historic photographs, and cultural exhibits that trace the archipelago's Swahili, Arab, and French influences.

train.note: There has never been a railway in the Comoros, on Grande Comore or any other island, so no train services exist and none are planned. Movement between the islands is by boat or on Int'Air Îles flights from Moroni's Prince Saïd Ibrahim airport, and travel on Grande Comore itself is entirely by road.

bus.note: The Comoros are islands, so no bus can cross a border and there are no international coach services. On Grande Comore, shared taxis and minibuses leave the Volo Volo market area in Moroni for villages around the island whenever they fill up; fares are paid in cash Comorian francs, there is no timetable or online booking, and the circuit of the island takes several hours. Hiring a car with a driver is the usual alternative.

intl.to: Mutsamudu, Anjouan (Comoros) & Dzaoudzi, Mayotte (France) - sails from Moroni port about twice a week
intl.op: SGTM, MV Maria Galanta — tickets at the SGTM office by Moroni port

intl.to: Fomboni, Mohéli & Mutsamudu, Anjouan (Comoros) - cargo vessels from Moroni port that also carry passengers, up to 12 hours
intl.op: local shipping agents — tickets at the port office

intl.to: Hoani, Mohéli (Comoros) - speedboats from Chindini on the south coast of Grande Comore, about 1 hour
intl.op: local boat owners — pay at the beach

ferry.note: Moroni has no deep-water quay, so passengers are tendered out to ships in small boats, which is uncomfortable in any swell. The Maria Galanta is the only scheduled passenger vessel, linking Moroni with Mutsamudu on Anjouan and Dzaoudzi on the French island of Mayotte roughly twice a week for around €36 to Anjouan - a French visa is required for Mayotte even though the crossing is short. The Chindini-Hoani speedboats are open fibreglass launches that run in the morning and only in calm weather, and they are effectively suspended during the kusi winds of roughly June to September. Nothing can be booked online, sailings are frequently cancelled, and cargo boats between the island capitals are cheap but very slow.
